item.title: Vespasian: The Commoner Who Became Roman Emperor
item.description: Though not as famous or dramatic as his colorful predecessors, Vespasian was one of the most important emperors of Rome. He came to power at the end of the Year of the Four Emperors, a time of great instability and upheaval for the empire; a commoner, he proved that an emperor was not necessarily born but made, through strength of arms. item.title: Akkad and the Akkadian Empire: The First Multinational Empire in the World
item.description: The city of Akkad was the seat of the Akkadian Empire (2350/2334-2154 BCE), the first multinational political entity in the world, founded by Sargon the Great, who unified Mesopotamia under his rule and set the model for later Mesopotamian kings to follow or attempt to surpass. The Akkadian Empire developed concepts invented by the Sumerians and introduced many of its own that would inform later dynasties and empires in the region.

item.title: Tiberius: The Reclusive Roman Emperor
item.description: Tiberius was the second emperor of Rome, who reigned from 14 to 37 CE. A gloomy and uncharismatic man, he had to fill the massive shoes of his stepfather, Augustus. In some ways, he proved equal to the task, but he often devolved into cruelty and aloofness, leaving the empire in the hands of power-hungry men like the Machiavellian Praetorian prefect Sejanus. Discover the tortured and tumultuous life of Rome's reclusive emperor.

item.title: Babylon: The Gate of the Gods
item.description: Babylon was a great cultural and religious center and, at its height, the largest city in the world. item.title: Year of the Four Emperors: When Four Men Battled For Control of the Roman Empire
item.description: January 69 CE. The tyrannical Emperor Nero is dead, having killed himself after being declared a public enemy by the Senate. In his place, the aged and unpopular Galba sits on the throne - but, with no blood ties to the now extinct House of Caesar, Galba's rule is precarious indeed. He is beset by pretenders on all sides. In Germany, the legions proclaim their own general, Vitellius, as emperor. In Judea, the general Vespasian watches events play out, waiting for an opportunity to make his move.

item.title: Battle of Isandlwana: The Zulu Victory over the British Empire
item.description: By 1878, the British were determined to create their federation of Southern Africa, but one serious obstacle remained: the Zulu Kingdom. The British were wary of a well-organised state so close to their frontiers, but the Zulus had, in fact, shown no signs of hostility to their European neighbours. item.title: The Making of the Middle Ages: An Atlas of Europe
item.description: An in-depth historical atlas that examines the history of Europe from circa 117 CE to 1000 CE. The focus of the book is not on the full period of medieval Europe but rather on how the Europe that we recognise today was formed during the early Middle Ages. It does so using fantastic maps, short and varied descriptive chapters, and many detailed illustrations.

item.title: The Heretic of Cacheu: Crispina Peres and the Struggle over Life in Seventeenth-Century West Africa
item.description: Toby Green’s "The Heretic of Cacheu: Crispina Peres and the Struggle over Life in Seventeenth-Century West Africa" is a richly detailed and deeply human book centered on the life of Crispina Peres, a powerful African woman trader prosecuted by the Portuguese Inquisition in the 1660s. The book opens a window onto the everyday realities, moral tensions, and global connections of early modern West Africa. The book will be of interest to historians of religion or gender and history enthusiasts.

item.title: The Legend of Sargon of Akkad: Inspiration for the Story of Moses
item.description: The Legend of Sargon of Akkad describes the king's humble origins and rise to power with the help of the goddess Ishtar and concludes with a challenge to future kings to go where he has gone and do as he has done. item.title: Secession of the Plebs: One of History's First Class Conflicts
item.description: In 494 BCE, the plebeians (commoners) protested their mistreatment by the ruling patrician class with a mass exodus from Rome. Leaving the patricians to fend for themselves, they set up camp on the Sacred Mountain three miles (5 km) away and forced the Senate to negotiate. Discover how Rome's plebeians won their rights through some of the first mass general strikes in Western history.
